[29 November 2002 ]
Well, it's finaly time to update this page. Some of the things that have changed are listed below.

  • Downgraded the binutils package to a more stable version. With newer verision of bison, the old binutils version would not compile without minor modifications.
  • Made some major improvements to the toolchain auto-build script. Updating the toolchain is now as easy as dumping the tar.gz file under the <sdk_path>/pkgs directory and modifying the auto-build scrip to point to the new file. Also if for some reason the auto-build script fails, it will resume where it left off. Before, it would start all over from the beginning.
  • The SDK has also seen some improvements. There now are 'install' and 'strip' wrappers for use in cygwin. The ones provide in cygwin fail when processing files with .exe extensions. Also from this point on, the SDK will hold a verison number.
  • Fixed a problem with the runtime libraries which contained absolute paths. This caused some initial installs to fail (Thanks Andrey for pointing this problem out).

USB/Serial/Power Adapter Schematic:

If you plan on doing any real hacking on the BE300, your going to need a serial cable. You can either buy one or build your own. If you decide to build your own, the following may prove useful.

  • serial-con.pdf (12k)

You will also need connectors which you can get from [ www.pc-mobile.net ] You'll need the Casio E1xx, EM500 - 20-pin (PCC01) ones.

Linux4BE SDK:

So you want to join in on the fun? Well the first things your going to need are the tools used in development. Below I outline 2 methods in which you can obtain them.

Option 1: Prebuilt Toolchain

This is the easyiest way, just download them here:

  • linux4be-tools-linux-2.4.18-20021129 ((51,504k) - Linux Environments
  • linux4be-tools-win32-2.4.18-20021129 (50,307k) - Win32/Cygwin Environment

To install, issue the following from a command shell in a directory of your choice. Note, cygwin installs must be done under a cygwin commmand shell, perferably bash, NOT the windows command shell.

bash$ tar xzvf linux4be-tools-<platform>-2.4.18-20021129.tar.gz
bash$ mv linux4be-tools-<platform>-2.4.18-20021129 xLinux4BE

Where <platform> is either linux or win32 ( depending on your platform ). To actually use the cross-toolchain, you must set your path as follows:

bash$ export PATH=<path-to-xLinux4BE>/bin:$PATH

You can also look here [TimeSys Linux for MIPS-based NEC VR4122 processor] for an alternate toolchain binary package. The instructions for installing it should be availiable there also.

Option 2: Roll Your Own

Grab the SDK and unpack it. The location is unimportant. Then grab the rest of the files for your particular environment and place them in the <sdk_path>/pkgs directory.

  • linux4be_sdk_20021129.tar.gz (7.16k) - All Environments
  • binutils-2.12.tar.gz (12,321k) - All Environments
  • gcc-3.0.4.tar.gz (18,004k) - All Environments
  • linux4be-2.4.18-20021129.tar.gz (31,177k) - All Environments
  • linux4be-ramdisk.gz (1,108k) - All Environments
  • linux4be-runtime-2.4.18-20021129.tar.gz (32,932k) - Win32/Cygwin Environment
  • glibc-2.2.4.tar.gz (16,023k) - Linux Environment
  • glibc-linuxthreads-2.2.4.tar.gz (215k) - Linux Environment

Once the needed packages have been downloaded, issue the following commands:

bash$ cd <sdk_path>
bash$ ./scripts/dotoolchain

And thats it. Depending on your hardware and environment, it could take anywhere from 1-4 hours to compile. On a 233MHz machine running Mandrake Linux it took about 2 1/2 hours. The toolchain will be installed at ~/toolchains/xLinux4BE.

BTW, if you want, you can email me the time/space requirements for your system and i post them here. It may help other with similar setups.

Now if you really like doing things the hard way you can bypass running the script above and instead follow this HOWTO . Note: A local copy of this is provided in the SDK.
